articles.headline: Micaela digs under Lima: the first underground metro
articles.standfirst: A big machine is helping to build Peru's first underground train.
body: Lima and Callao are building the first underground metro in Peru. This week, the President of Peru, Keiko Fujimori, visited the work in the district of Carmen de la Legua. She saw a big machine called Micaela arrive. The machine digs a tunnel under the city.

The workers have finished digging the places for all the stations on Line 2 and on a branch of Line 4. The President said that the metro will save people a lot of time. Today, many people spend three or four hours every day in minibuses and buses to go to work and come back home.
She said that this time should be for families. She also thanked the engineers and technicians from Peru and other countries who worked on the first part of the metro.

articles.headline: Take a photo, help a beach
articles.standfirst: A phone and a small stand help scientists to watch the coast.
body: A beach changes every day. Big waves take sand away, and calm weather brings sand back. Scientists want to see these changes, but it is hard work to watch every beach all the time.

Now people can help with a phone. The project is called CoastSnap. It started in Australia in 2017. At a CoastSnap place, there is a small stand for your phone and a sign. You put your phone on the stand, take a photo and send it to the scientists.

The stand makes sure that every photo is taken from nearly the same place. Then a computer program changes the photos into a view from above and finds the line of the sea on the sand. There are now more than 200 CoastSnap places in 21 countries.

articles.headline: Time off for a big visit: Peru plans special days for Pope Leo XIV
articles.standfirst: A new decree gives many workers extra non-working days in November, but the hours must be made up.
body: Pope Leo XIV is going to visit Peru from 11 to 16 November, and the government wants to make it easier for people to take part. On 23 October it published a decree, signed by President Keiko Fujimori, that declares special non-working days for workers in both the public and the private sectors.

The days are different in each part of the country. In Lima and Callao, workers will be free from 1 p.m. on 11 and 12 November, and for the whole of 16 November. In Cajamarca, La Libertad, Lambayeque and Piura, the days are 13 and 14 November. In the private sector, Cusco and Ucayali will also have 15 November.

A non-working day is not the same as a public holiday. People do not have to work, but they must make up the hours later. In the public sector, the hours must be recovered within ten days, or at a time chosen by the head of each office. In the private sector, the company and its workers must agree how to do it. If they cannot agree, the employer decides.

The decree says that the visit has a special spiritual, historical and social importance for the country. It also says that services which are essential for the community must continue to work on those days.

articles.headline: Two strong earthquakes shake the sea near Vanuatu
articles.standfirst: A tsunami warning was issued for coasts near the centre of the quakes.
body: Two strong earthquakes struck the sea near Vanuatu, a country of islands in the South Pacific, on Saturday afternoon. The first one had a magnitude of 6.9, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS). It happened about 200 kilometres west of the town of Sola, at a depth of 10 kilometres. A second earthquake, with a magnitude of 6.3, followed shortly after.

After the earthquakes, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Centre said that dangerous waves were possible on coasts within 300 kilometres of the centre of the quake. A tsunami is a series of very big sea waves that an earthquake under the ocean can cause. The warning centre's first forecast named Vanuatu as the area that could be affected.

At first, the warning centre gave the larger earthquake a magnitude of 7.2, but the USGS lowered the number to 6.9. Early measurements can change when scientists get more information, so the first number is not always the final one.

The centre asked people in threatened coastal areas to stay alert and to follow the instructions of national and local authorities. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology said that there was no threat to Australia. Vanuatu is in the Ring of Fire, an area around the Pacific Ocean where earthquakes are common.

articles.headline: Higher prices, bigger shipments: Peru's mining exports leap by 55%
articles.standfirst: Copper and gold drive a record-style rise, but the good news depends partly on world markets.
body: Peru's mining exports are growing at a remarkable pace. According to the National Society of Mining, Petroleum and Energy (SNMPE), they reached $57.492 billion between January and August 2026, which is 55% more than the $37.081 billion earned in the same months of 2025. Mining alone accounted for 74.3% of everything Peru sold abroad in that period. The result is a clear sign that the sector remains the engine of the country's foreign trade.

Two metals explain most of the increase. Copper exports totalled $26.513 billion, up 54.8% on last year, and made up 46.1% of the value of mining exports. Gold shipments reached $21.631 billion, a rise of 58%, or 37.6% of the total. In absolute terms, copper added $9.388 billion to the annual comparison, gold added $7.938 billion and lead $2.019 billion.

August shows how the rise works. Mining exports that month came to $7.858 billion, 52.1% more than in August 2025. The SNMPE said that copper's 56% growth was driven by a 38.1% increase in the price of the metal and a 13% increase in the volume exported. For gold, a 31% rise in price was combined with a 14.1% increase in volume. In other words, higher prices and larger shipments worked together, and neither factor alone explains the jump.

The figures show a double effect: Peru is selling more metal, and it is selling it at higher prices. That is encouraging for a country whose economy depends heavily on mining, but it also means that the result is partly out of Peru's hands, since international prices can fall as quickly as they rise. For that reason, economists often argue that countries exposed to a few raw materials should use periods of high income to develop other sectors of their economy.

articles.headline: A patient's petition, 137 cheaper drugs: India caps cancer-medicine mark-ups
articles.standfirst: A court case begun by a retired bank clerk has pushed the government to act.
body: India has announced that 137 cancer drugs will become cheaper from next month, after a legal case started by an ordinary patient. Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a retired bank clerk in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Her treatment cost more than 63,000 rupees a month (about £500), far more than her family could pay. In 2022 she asked the Kerala high court to make the government act. She did not live to see the result, but the case reached the supreme court.

The judges examined how much hospitals, distributors and pharmacies add to the price of medicines, and they described the situation in the strongest terms, calling the mark-ups 'extortion'. In one example, a drug sold to hospitals for 2,700 rupees was priced at 27,000 rupees. An official study found that the average trade mark-up on some cancer drugs was 170%, and in extreme cases more than 700%.

A cap of 30% on the trade margin already existed for 42 drugs. The government has now extended it to 137 more. It expects prices to fall by up to 70% and patients to save around 2,500 crore rupees (£199m) every year.

Not everyone is convinced that this is enough. Campaigners expect companies and hospitals to look for loopholes, for instance by raising charges for other services to replace the lost income. Jyotsna Singh, from a network that campaigns for access to medicines, called for a complete reform of the system and for transparency along the whole supply chain. The supreme court has also asked why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not to all medicines without a patent. The government has until 27 October to reply.

The problem is large. India records about 1.56 million new cancer cases a year, up from 1.39 million in 2020, and studies suggest that health spending pushes about 55 million Indians below the poverty line every year.

articles.headline: A potato-shaped moon and a very light touch: Japan sets out to bring back a piece of Phobos
articles.standfirst: The MMX spacecraft has left Earth on the first mission to collect samples from a moon of Mars.
body: On Monday, Japan's space agency JAXA launched a rocket from the Tanegashima Space Centre carrying the Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, known as MMX. It is the first mission designed to bring back material from a moon of Mars, and the opening stage of a five-year, international project.

The target is Phobos, a moon that no spacecraft has ever explored on its surface. MMX will spend about a year travelling to the Martian system, where it is due to arrive in 2027, and will then enter a quasi-satellite orbit, a path that keeps it close to Phobos. After a period of observation, it will attempt two soft landings. On the way, MMX will also take photographs of Mars and of Phobos, images that its team is eagerly waiting to see.

The great difficulty is the weak gravity of Phobos. Yaji Kentaro, from the MMX team, explained that engineers had feared a landing vehicle might simply tip over, so its legs have been given special features to keep it stable. The vehicle is to collect at least ten grams of sand from a depth of about two centimetres.

Why go to such lengths? Mars today is a cold desert with a thin atmosphere, yet scientists believe its environment was once similar to Earth's, and traces of water have been found there. The mission hopes to shed light on the origin of water and organic matter on Mars and on how the planet and its moons formed. JAXA also thinks that this 'potato-shaped' moon could contain material thrown off the surface of Mars long ago, possibly including evidence of ancient life. According to Yaji, the answer to where the water and organic matter needed for life came from may be hidden in the samples.

Once the samples have been collected, the spacecraft will observe Deimos, the second Martian moon, and then begin a year-long journey home. The capsule is expected to land in South Australia. The project is also regarded as a stepping stone towards possible human exploration of the Martian system in the future.

articles.headline: Shirts that mean more than a jersey: how Pasifika fans are reshaping the Rugby League World Cup
articles.standfirst: Samoa and Tonga once played in the shadow of bigger teams. Now they fill the stadiums.
body: A Friday workday, a kick-off at 5.45 p.m., traffic jammed across western Sydney and a match that was bound to be one-sided: on paper, it was a poor moment to attract a crowd. Yet 13,000 people filled Western Sydney Stadium to watch Samoa beat France 78–4 in the men's Rugby League World Cup, Samoa's biggest win ever, and they sang a traditional song of thanks. Even after the final siren, Benaiah Ioelu scored one more try when a penalty kick hit the post and bounced back to him.

It was not an isolated case. Fiji's game against the Cook Islands in Newcastle drew just over 10,000 spectators and 1.7 million television viewers across Australia, more than several flagship news and current affairs programmes. The meeting of Samoa and Tonga on 1 November was the first match of the tournament to sell out, and former players have asked for it to be moved from a 30,000-seat stadium to the larger Stadium Australia.

Behind this lies demography. The number of Australians who identify with Pasifika communities almost tripled in a decade, from 165,000 in 2011 to 415,033 in 2021, with large communities in the outer suburbs of Sydney and Brisbane. Sierra Keung, a sports academic at Auckland University of Technology, was not surprised by the turnout: for these communities, she said, a team shirt is far more than a piece of clothing.

A rule change in 2017 also helped, because it allowed players with cultural ties to several nations to choose which one to represent. Jason Taumalolo's decision to play for Tonga was the best-known example. Of the starting line-up that beat Lebanon 36–0, none was born in Tonga, but all have family roots there. Lebanon's team follows a similar logic: its players were all born in Australia, and its coach, Michael Cheika, is Lebanese Australian.

Australia's Kangaroos have won twelve world titles, including six of the last seven, yet observers now suggest that their long dominance could be under threat. As heritage rather than birthplace increasingly decides who plays for whom, the tournament may belong above all to the diasporas that have given it a new energy.

cartoons.title: Good luck, Bea

image.alt: Three panels: Bea is nervous about her school play, Byte offers a bandage and says 'break a leg', and Bea explains that it means good luck.

transcript.speaker: Bea
transcript.text: The school play is tonight. I am so nervous!

transcript.speaker: Byte
transcript.text: Then I will keep the bandage. Just in case.

cartoons.explanation: 'Break a leg' is a friendly way to say 'good luck', especially before a performance. Byte understands the words literally, so he arrives with a bandage. The joke is that he still keeps it at the end, just in case.

glossary.def: An expression that means 'good luck', often used before a show.

cartoons.title: I agree

image.alt: Four panels: Byte claims to have read fourteen thousand words in two seconds, Bea asks what they say, Byte clicks 'I agree' confidently, and Bea discovers he has ordered 200 pineapples a month.

transcript.speaker: Byte
transcript.text: Fourteen thousand words of terms and conditions. I read them all in two seconds.

transcript.speaker: Byte
transcript.text: No idea. But I ticked 'I agree' with great confidence.

transcript.speaker: Bea
transcript.text: What exactly did you agree to?

cartoons.explanation: Byte confuses reading with understanding: he has scanned every word but cannot say what any of them mean. The joke exaggerates something real, which is that many people click 'I agree' without reading the terms. The pineapples make the consequence absurd, and Byte's confidence makes it funnier.

glossary.def: The rules that you accept when you use a service or buy something online.
In a very sure way, even if you are not sure of the facts.
Used to say that something seems to be true, but you have only just found out.

cartoons.prompt: B2: Do you read the terms and conditions before you accept them online? Write 40–60 words explaining why or why not. C1: Explain why Byte's claim in the first panel is both true and meaningless, and what the strip suggests about 'informed consent' (70–100 words).
cartoons.discussion: A possible reading is that the strip is about the gap between access to information and real understanding. Byte can process every word, yet he has no judgement about which words matter. It also criticises how digital services are designed: terms are so long that agreeing becomes a ritual, not a choice, and the person who clicks may be as unaware of the result as Byte is.
